units: the steam produced while cooking moves through the room
on touching the cold glass this steam turns back into liquid
the water left on the pane blocks the view outside
the condensed water slides down and gathers at the bottom of the window
standing water swells the wood and lifts the paint
an unpleasant smell ends up spreading through the kitchen
the root of the trouble is the moisture made inside the home
changing the air while cooking breaks the process
it is better to open up before the film appears than after
text: Steam rising from a pot of boiling water does not simply vanish into thin air. It drifts across the room until it meets the cold glass of the window. Against that chilled surface it turns back into water and leaves a thick film that blurs whatever lies outside. The droplets slide down the pane and gather along the bottom rail of the frame. Let them sit there and the wood swells, the paint lifts in blisters, and a sour smell works its way through the kitchen. So the fault does not lie with the rain falling outside. It lies with the damp air that people make themselves while they cook. Open a window while the pans are on and the chain breaks: wet air leaves, dry air comes in, and the condensation has nothing left to feed on. Anyone who has learned that opens up before the panes turn white, not afterward, once the damage has taken hold.

units: a sharp knock came with every closing of the kitchen cabinet
the door struck the frame instead of settling flat
the tenant first suspected that the wood had warped
sanding the edge changed nothing
a lamp held close revealed play in the upper hinge
the screws were spinning in holes that had grown too wide
glued wood splinters made it possible to build a solid grip again
once dry the screws went back into fresh material
the door closes quietly again
the episode shows that the source of a noise rarely sits where the ear places it
text: A sharp knock came every evening as the kitchen cabinet was shut: the left door struck the frame instead of settling flat against it. The tenant blamed the wood first, certain that damp had crept in and warped the panel. She sanded the edge back with care. Nothing changed. Then she held a lamp close to the joint and saw it at once. The upper hinge had worked loose, two screws were spinning freely in a hole that had widened around them, and the door hung askew. A cabinetmaker's trick fixed it: pack the tired holes with splinters of wood soaked in glue, let them set hard, then drive the screws into fresh material. Since then the door swings shut without a sound and the handle no longer scrapes the frame beside it. The whole business left her with a rule. When furniture complains, the source is rarely where your ear puts it.

units: the two cleaning cloths do not serve the same purpose
the kitchen cloth is thin and dries without leaving marks
the kitchen cloth suits dishes and cooking surfaces
the floor cloth soaks up a large puddle
the floor cloth leaves a damp film behind it
the two must be stored apart
the floor cloth needs rinsing in scalding water after use or it will smell
the kitchen cloth goes into the machine with the rest of the wash
the deciding test is contact with food
text: Want to clean fast and clean well? Start by telling your two helpers apart, because they were never meant for the same job. The dish towel is thin and tightly woven; it holds little water but wipes dry without leaving streaks, so keep it for plates, glasses, and the cooking surface. The floor cloth is thick and loose. It drinks up a whole puddle, yet it leaves a damp film behind wherever it passes, and it belongs to the floor, never the table. Get into the habit of storing them apart, one folded in a drawer, the other hanging over the bucket. Rinse the floor cloth in scalding water after every pass, or it holds on to a stale smell. The towel goes into the machine with the sheets. One last test, the only one to keep if the rest slips away: ask whether the surface touches food. Yes, take the towel. No, take the other.

units: a group has set up a repair workshop in an old covered market
a first bench is given over to clothes and cloth accessories
trousers are taken up there and fallen hems are stitched back
a second bench handles electrical devices
damaged power cords make up most of the electrical requests
a third bench looks after furniture
legs are glued back there and fittings or handles are replaced
a fourth space lends out tools for a modest membership
the waiting line has not grown shorter since the opening
a mobile service is planned for outlying districts
text: Inside an old covered market, a local group has opened a workshop where things once thrown out are given a second life. The first bench takes in cloth: a pair of trousers shortened, a fallen hem stitched back into place, a torn bag strap swapped for another one. The second is kept for electrical devices, and broken power cords make up most of what comes through the door. The third, far noisier than the rest, works on furniture: a loose leg glued back on, a hinge reset, a fresh handle screwed into place. A quieter fourth corner runs as a tool library, where anyone can borrow a drill in return for a small membership. The volunteers press one point above all others. The line has not grown any shorter since the doors first opened, which says the know-how is missing more than the will. A mobile service is due to reach the outlying districts before long.

units: at sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone
washing done the day before hangs on a line strung between two walls
the water dripping from the washing runs into a groove cut in the ground
by midday the air dries out and the sheets swell
a cat settles on the warm rim of the well
a wooden panel bangs on an upper floor before falling back against the wall
late in the afternoon a neighbor comes for her washing
she leaves the pins clipped to the line
in the evening the courtyard empties and a smell of soap lingers
night brings the damp back onto the flagstones
text: At sunrise the inner courtyard still smells of wet stone. Yesterday's wash sags on a line strung between two walls, and the water falls drop by drop into a narrow groove cut along the paving. Toward midday the air dries out, and the sheets swell and snap like sails. A gray cat settles on the warm rim of the well, its eyes half closed against the light. A wooden shutter bangs on an upper floor, then falls back slackly against the wall. Late in the afternoon a neighbor comes down for her wash, folds each piece over her arm, and leaves the pins clipped to the line behind her. Once evening comes the courtyard empties, the groove dries out, and nothing is left but a smell of soap hanging between the walls. Then night brings its chill, the damp creeps back onto the flagstones, and the courtyard quietly gets ready to begin the round again.

units: welding a casing shut instead of screwing it down cuts off access to the inner parts
with no access the independent shop cannot work out what has failed
with no diagnosis no price is quoted
the owner ends up buying a replacement device
each step of the reasoning looks sound taken on its own
the sequence leads to throwing out an object that a minor part would have saved
as repairers grow scarce the handing on of technical skill breaks off
the know-how is missing where demand is rising
the useful move is on design and not on sorting waste
text: Turning a repair away costs far more than it looks, and the mechanism is worth setting out with some care. A maker who welds a casing shut instead of screwing it down cuts off every route to the parts inside. With no way in, the independent shop cannot work out what has failed. With no diagnosis, it will not quote a price. With no quote, the owner goes and buys a replacement. Each link looks sound on its own, and the whole chain ends with a discarded object that one hinge or one seal would have kept in use. A second effect runs beneath it, harder to see: as repairers grow scarce, the handing on of technical skill breaks off, so the know-how is missing at the very place where demand keeps rising. Reversing that means working upstream, on how devices are designed, rather than downstream, on how the waste is sorted.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the alterations seamstress keeps a narrow shop in a neighborhood
she began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop
she put linings together there one after another
the closing of the workshop left her without a job
she owned only a secondhand machine and had no customers
she changed scale by mending single pieces instead of producing runs
each repair costs less than a replacement garment
her order book shows a wait of two weeks
she is handing the trade on to an apprentice
text: Behind a narrow shopfront, the neighborhood seamstress keeps up a trade that most people had written off. She began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop, running linings together one after another, day after day. When that workshop closed its doors she was left without a job, holding a secondhand machine and not a single customer of her own. Her answer was to change scale. Rather than sew long runs, she offered to rescue single pieces instead. A hem taken up, a sandal strap sewn back on, a pocket restitched, a broken fastener swapped out: every job of that kind costs less than the garment it saves. Her shop is never empty and her order book shows a wait of two weeks. She has taken on an apprentice of her own, sure that the trade dies unless it is handed over out loud, with a hand laid on the work.

units: two clothes racks are sold in the same place at very different prices
the steel model opens easily and carries a heavy load
its feet skid on a smooth floor
the aluminum model weighs half as much
the aluminum model packs into a slim sleeve
its drying surface is smaller
the heavy one suits large households
the light one suits cramped homes
one corrodes at the joints and the other bends under a wet load
the choice turns on the room the buyer has
text: Two clothes racks share the same shelf and carry a wide gap in price between them, yet daily use settles the matter far less sharply than the packaging claims. The first, in coated steel, opens out with a single pull and takes a heavy load without sagging in the middle. Its side wings lock on a firm catch, but its feet skid on a smooth floor. The second, in aluminum, weighs half as much and packs away into a slim sleeve, which suits a cramped home. Its drying surface stays smaller, though, and two sheets barely fit on it at once. Put to work, the heavy one serves a large household while the light one serves a small place. Neither deserves the enthusiasm of its own leaflet: one corrodes at the joints, the other bows its bars under a wet towel. What settles the choice, above all else, is the room the buyer has to spare.

units: the writer of the message is leaving and gives instructions to the housemate
the kitchen faucet drips if it is shut too sharply
a tool for pouring oil sits under the sink
the wardrobe door has to be lifted to close
a hanger for a coat has been cleared
the hot water takes a while before it can be used
the mailbox fills up fast and has to be emptied
the recycling bag has to go out at the start of the week
the neighbor below knocks on the ceiling when people walk heavily in the evening
that neighbor sleeps while the residents are awake
text: Hey, I head off tonight, so here is how the place works, with nothing left out I hope. Kitchen: the faucet drips if you shut it too sharply, so turn it slowly, and the funnel for oil sits under the sink beside the floor cloth. Bedroom: the wardrobe closes badly, you have to lift the door as you push it, and I have cleared a hanger for your coat. Bathroom: the water heater takes an age to warm up, so switch it on well before you undress. Mail: the box fills up fast, so empty it on your way in and leave the lot on the low table. The recycling bag goes out at the start of the week, so remember to carry it down. One more thing, the man below knocks on his ceiling as soon as anyone walks heavily after the evening meal. Do not hold it against him, he sleeps while the rest of us are still up.

units: a building caretaker describes how his week runs
he starts at first light with the cleaning of the shared areas
he checks the lighting in the stairwell
he puts the bins out before the collection truck comes
he brings the washed bins back once the collection is done
the lower fitting on the bike room door gives way regularly
he straightens that door every other week
he gives a whole stretch of time to repairs reported by the residents
he makes a round at the end of the day to check the locks
he reckons that the steadiness of the routine keeps him going
text: We asked the building caretaker to walk us through his week, one task at a time. He starts at first light with the shared areas: sweeping the hall, running a mop across the entrance, checking the bulbs in the stairwell. Asked what follows, he explains that he wheels the bins out before the truck arrives, then brings them back washed once the collection has moved on. We ask him which problem turns up most often. He names the bike room door, whose lower hinge gives way under the weight and which he has to straighten every other week. Midweek he gives a whole stretch of time to the repairs that residents have reported. Then comes the evening round, when he tries every lock in turn. Asked whether the work tires him out, he answers that the steady routine keeps him going more than it wears him down.
